newsitem.title: UK: UK sees OTC drug court case in late 97 at earliest.
newsitem.headline: UK sees OTC drug court case in late 97 at earliest.

text.p: Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT) said it expected its advice to remove resale price maintenance (RPM) on over-the-counter drugs only to come to court by late 1997 at the earliest.
"This is not going to happen today. I think it is unlikely the court will consider it before late 1997 or early 1998," OFT head John Bridgeman told reporters.
He said it was not a foregone conclusion that removal of the RPM would on balance lead to closures of local pharmacists, who would not have the muscle to compete with aggressive supermarket chains.
"This (any RPM removal) is also going to be an opportunity for new pharmacies to open up as well," Bridgeman said.
"This is the opportunity for the enterpreneurial pharmacists to use his negotiating power to put presssure on the manufacturers and the wholesalers," he added.

A 1970 court order currently allows drug producers to set and enforce minimum prices for non-prescription medicines, but the OFT argues trading conditions have changed so much since that it is time to abolish the retail price maintenance.

One of the main reasons to allow a price limit in 1970 was to protect pharmacists at a time when many were getting out of business across the country. But, said Bridgeman, at the moment there are more pharmacists opening up than closing their shops.
The OFT also asked for removal of the RPM on branded over-the-counter medicines because these drugs now make up far less of pharmacists profits than in the early 1970's, he added.
In a further attempt to ease worries over the effects of more competition in drugs retailing, the OFT chief pointed to the smooth introduction of free pricing for prescription drugs in the mid 1970s.
"There were a lot of concerns when the RPM collapsed for prescription prices, but there haven't been any adverse consequences," Bridgeman said.
The OFT's advice follows a campaign by supermarket group ASDA which maintained that branded OTC drugs were too expensive and consistently priced its own comparable goods at lower prices.
